title: Online Customer Support
subtitle: Handle customer chats, emails and complaints professionally, track every case and prove your results with real support metrics.
description: A practical course in written customer support on WhatsApp Business, email and chat. You will set up your tools, write clear replies and templates, calm angry customers, track tickets in a simple sheet or free help desk, calculate metrics such as first response time and resolution rate, and build a portfolio for remote support work.
outcomes: Set up WhatsApp Business with a profile, greeting and away messages, quick replies and status labels
Handle any request with a six-step workflow and write clear, warm replies and templates
De-escalate angry customers using the LAST method and handle scams and safety complaints correctly
Track tickets in a spreadsheet or free help-desk tool and calculate first response time, resolution rate, FCR and CSAT
Build a support portfolio and a 90-day improvement plan, and apply safely for remote support roles
audience: Women who answer customers for their own business or someone else's, or who want a remote customer support job, and can already use WhatsApp and basic email.
tools: Smartphone with the free WhatsApp Business app (a separate SIM is ideal)
Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel (free Google Sheets works on a phone)
Optional: laptop and a free help-desk plan such as Freshdesk

modules.title: Foundations: channels, setup and safety
modules.overview: Understand how written customer support works on WhatsApp, email and chat, set up your tools so you reply faster and more consistently, and protect customers' data and money from day one.

lessons.title: How online support works: channels, customers and your role
objectives: Explain what online customer support is and how it differs from face-to-face service
Compare WhatsApp Business, email and website or social media chat as support channels
Choose the right channel for a given type of customer request
Describe the three promises every support reply must keep: speed, clarity and follow-through

blocks.text: Online customer support means helping customers in writing, through a screen, instead of across a counter. The customer cannot see your smile or hear your voice. Everything they feel about the business comes from **how fast you reply, what your words say, and whether you do what you promised**. In this course you will learn to do that well, on the channels Nigerian customers really use, and to keep simple records that show your work.

A support request is any message where a customer needs something: a question before buying ("Do you deliver to Ibadan?"), a problem after buying ("My order has not arrived"), a change ("Please change the size to 42") or a complaint ("The cream you sent is leaking"). Your job is to understand the request, solve it or pass it to the right person, and tell the customer clearly what happens next.

blocks.name: instant-support
blocks.alt: A support agent answering a customer chat on a screen
blocks.caption: Online support is written support: your reply speed and wording are the whole customer experience.

blocks.text: The three main channels
Most small and medium businesses in Nigeria support customers through three kinds of channel. Each one has strengths and weaknesses, so a good agent knows when to use which.

head: Channel
Best for
Watch out for
rows: WhatsApp Business
Quick questions, order updates, sending photos and voice notes, customers who prefer their phone
Messages pile up fast; easy to forget to reply; personal and business chats can get mixed on one phone
Email
Formal complaints, refunds, invoices, anything that needs a clear written record or attachments
Customers expect a complete, well-structured answer; slower back-and-forth
Website or social media chat (for example Instagram or Facebook messages, or a chat box on a website)
Customers who are already browsing; quick pre-sale questions
Customers expect near-instant replies while they are still on the page

blocks.text: Some businesses also take phone calls. This course focuses on written support, but the same habits apply: listen, confirm, solve, record.
Matching the request to the channel

A simple rule: **keep quick things quick, and move serious things to a record**. A customer who asks the price of a bag on WhatsApp should get the answer on WhatsApp. A customer who wants a refund of ₦45,000 should still get a fast, warm reply on WhatsApp, but the refund details (order number, amount, bank details for the refund, date promised) should be confirmed in writing in a way the business can find again, for example by email or in your tracking sheet.

items: **Pre-sale question** (price, size, delivery area): answer on the same channel, quickly.
**Order status** ("Where is my order?"): check the record first, then reply with a specific date or step.
**Problem or complaint**: acknowledge fast, collect details, log it, give a time for the next update.
**Money matters** (refunds, double payment): confirm details in writing and follow the business's approval rule. Never promise money you are not allowed to approve.

blocks.title: Worked example: one morning's messages
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi supports a small skincare brand in Enugu. At 9:00 am she opens WhatsApp Business and finds 6 unread chats and 1 email.
steps: She scans all 7 first instead of answering the top one. 3 are price questions, 1 is "Where is my order?", 1 is a customer saying a jar arrived cracked, 1 is a wholesale enquiry, and the email is a refund request.
She answers the 3 price questions in about 5 minutes using saved replies (you will build these in Lesson 1.2).
For the order question she checks her sheet, sees the parcel left on Monday with the dispatch rider, and replies with the expected delivery day.
For the cracked jar she replies at once: she apologises, asks for a photo and the order number, and promises an update by 2:00 pm.
She forwards the wholesale enquiry to the owner with a one-line summary, and tells the customer the owner will reply today.
She acknowledges the refund email, logs it, and asks the owner for approval.
blocks.result: All 7 customers had a first reply within 30 minutes. The two serious cases were logged with a promised update time, so nothing was forgotten.

blocks.title: From message to closed case
items: Message arrives
Acknowledge quickly
Understand and check
Solve or escalate
Confirm with customer
Log and close
blocks.caption: Every request, on any channel, should move through these six stages.

blocks.text: Your three promises

Customers judge support on three things. **Speed**: a quick first reply, even if it only says you are checking. **Clarity**: short sentences, specific facts, a clear next step. **Follow-through**: if you say "I will update you by 2 pm", you update them by 2 pm, even if the news is "still waiting". Breaking a promise does more damage than a slow first reply.

blocks.title: Support is a real job skill
blocks.text: Many businesses hire people to handle chats and emails, some full-time and some remotely. The skills in this course (clear writing, calm handling of complaints, organised records and simple metrics) are what employers look for. Module 4 covers how to present them.

Throughout this course you will build a small **support toolkit**: a set of saved replies, a tracking sheet, a list of escalation rules and a short report. By the end you will use these on real or realistic conversations and put them in a portfolio.

takeaways: Online support is judged on speed, clarity and follow-through.
WhatsApp suits quick questions; email suits records, refunds and formal complaints.
Scan all new messages first, then prioritise problems and money matters.
Every case should end with a confirmation and a record.

activity.title: Map your support channels
steps: List every channel customers use to contact the business you support (or a business you know well).
For each channel, write two typical requests that arrive there.
Mark which requests are quick questions, problems, or money matters.
Write one sentence for each channel saying what a good first reply time would be for that business.
activity.evidence: A one-page channel map (paper or phone note) with channels, typical requests and target first-reply times.

lessons.title: Setting up WhatsApp Business and email for support
objectives: Set up a WhatsApp Business profile with hours, address and a clear description
Create greeting and away messages and a set of quick replies
Use labels to sort chats by status
Write a professional email signature and a clear subject-line pattern

blocks.text: Good support starts before the first message arrives. A tidy setup saves you minutes on every chat and stops customers from asking the same basic questions again and again. In this lesson you will set up the two tools most small businesses rely on: the free **WhatsApp Business** app and an email account.

blocks.name: mobile-phone
blocks.caption: Most of your support work will happen on a phone, so set it up carefully once.

blocks.text: WhatsApp Business: the features that matter for support

WhatsApp Business is a separate free app from ordinary WhatsApp, made for small businesses. It runs on its own number, so many businesses use a dedicated SIM for it. That keeps customer chats away from family chats and lets another staff member take over the number if needed.

head: Feature
What it does
How you use it in support
rows: Business profile
Shows business name, category, description, address, hours, email and website
Answers "Where are you?" and "Are you open?" before customers ask
Greeting message
An automatic welcome sent to new customers when they first message
Sets expectations: who you are and how soon you reply
Away message
An automatic reply outside the hours you choose
Tells night-time customers when you will reply
Quick replies
Saved messages you insert by typing / and a shortcut word
Fast, consistent answers to repeated questions
Labels
Coloured tags on chats, such as New order or Pending
See at a glance which chats still need action
Catalogue
Product list with photos and prices
Send a product link instead of typing details

blocks.text: Menu names can change a little between app updates and between Android and iPhone. Look for these features under **Business tools** in the app's settings.
Writing your automatic messages
Automatic messages should be short, warm and honest. Never promise an instant answer if you cannot give one.

items: **Greeting:** "Hello, welcome to Ada's Kitchen 👋. Thank you for your message. Please tell us your name and what you need, and we will reply within 30 minutes during opening hours (Mon to Sat, 8 am to 6 pm)."
**Away:** "Thank you for your message. We are closed now and will reply from 8 am tomorrow. For orders, please send the item name, quantity and delivery area so we can help you faster."

blocks.text: Building quick replies
Look at the last 50 messages you received and note the questions that repeat. Each repeated question deserves a quick reply. Keep shortcut words simple so you remember them.

head: Shortcut
Saved message (example)
rows: /price
Thank you for asking. The 500 ml bottle is ₦4,500 and the 1 litre is ₦8,000 (prices as of this month). Which one would you like?
/delivery
We deliver within Lagos in 1 to 2 working days. Delivery is paid on arrival and depends on your area. Please send your area so we can confirm the fee.
/payment
You can pay by bank transfer to our business account only. We will never ask you to pay into a personal account. Please send your payment receipt here after paying.
/checking
Thank you for your patience. I am checking this now and will update you by [time].

blocks.title: Personalise every saved reply
blocks.text: A quick reply is a starting point, not a robot answer. Add the customer's name and adjust details before you press send. "Hello Tunde, thank you for asking" feels very different from a pasted block.
Labels as a simple to-do list

Create four labels and use them every day: **New**, **Waiting for customer**, **Waiting for us**, **Resolved**. At the end of each day, open the "Waiting for us" label. Any chat still there is a promise you have not kept yet.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting up in one evening
blocks.context: For example, Halima runs support for a fabric shop in Kano and has 1 hour to set up the business number.
steps: 10 minutes: business profile completed with category, opening hours (9 am to 6 pm), shop address and a two-line description.
10 minutes: greeting and away messages written and switched on, away message set to run outside opening hours.
25 minutes: she reads old chats and finds 6 repeated questions (price per yard, delivery, payment, minimum order, colours available, opening hours). She saves 6 quick replies.
10 minutes: she creates 4 labels and labels the 12 open chats.
5 minutes: she tests every quick reply by sending it to a friend's phone.
blocks.result: In the following week Halima estimates she saves several minutes per chat, and every customer gets the same correct price and payment instructions.

blocks.title: Support-ready setup
items: Profile and hours complete
Greeting message on
Away message on
Quick replies saved
Labels created
Email signature added
blocks.caption: Tick all six before you start handling real customers.

blocks.text: Email basics for support

For email, set a signature with your first name, role, business name, phone or WhatsApp number and working hours. Use a clear subject pattern so you and the customer can find the thread later, for example **"Order 1045: replacement for cracked jar"**. Keep one email thread per case; do not start a new email for every update.

blocks.title: Personal phone, business data
blocks.text: If the support number is on your personal phone, set a screen lock and do not let others browse it. Customer names, addresses and payment receipts are private information you are responsible for. Lesson 1.3 covers this.

takeaways: Use a separate WhatsApp Business number for support where possible.
Greeting and away messages set expectations; keep them honest about reply times.
Quick replies give speed and consistency, but always personalise them.
Four labels (New, Waiting for customer, Waiting for us, Resolved) work as a daily to-do list.

activity.title: Build your support setup
steps: Complete the WhatsApp Business profile for the business (or a practice business).
Write and switch on a greeting and an away message.
Save at least 5 quick replies for the most common questions.
Create the four status labels.
Add a professional email signature.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your profile, automatic messages, quick reply list and labels.

lessons.title: Protecting customers: privacy, scams and boundaries
objectives: Handle customer personal data in line with basic data protection principles
Recognise common scams aimed at businesses and customers on chat
Write safe payment and verification messages
Set professional boundaries for working hours and abusive messages

blocks.text: Support agents see a lot of private information: names, phone numbers, home addresses, payment receipts, sometimes ID or medical details. In Nigeria, the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** sets rules for how organisations collect and use personal data, and it is overseen by the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)**. You do not need to be a lawyer, but you must follow the basic principles: collect only what you need, use it only for the reason you collected it, keep it secure, and do not share it without a proper reason.

blocks.name: private-data
blocks.alt: A person protecting private data on a screen
blocks.caption: Customer data belongs to the customer; you are only looking after it.

blocks.text: Everyday privacy rules for agents

items: Ask only for what you need. To deliver an order you need a name, phone number and address. You do not need a date of birth.
Never post a customer's chat, receipt or address in a group or on a status, even as a joke or "lesson". If you use a real chat in your portfolio, remove names, numbers and addresses.
Do not discuss one customer's order with another person unless the customer has said that person can collect or ask.
Lock your phone and laptop. Log out of shared computers.
Delete or archive old files you no longer need, following the business's rule.

blocks.text: Scams you will meet on support channels
Scammers target both customers and businesses. A trained agent spots them and protects everyone.

head: Scam pattern
What it looks like
Safe response
rows: Fake payment alert
A "customer" sends a screenshot or SMS alert and asks you to release goods quickly
Confirm the money has landed in the business account (bank app or owner) before releasing anything
Overpayment and refund
"I sent ₦50,000 instead of ₦5,000 by mistake, please refund ₦45,000"
Check the real account balance first; refunds only after confirmed receipt and owner approval
Impersonating your business
Someone copies your name and logo and asks your customers to pay into a personal account
Tell customers your only official payment account in your quick replies and profile; report fake accounts
Asking for codes
"Please send me the 6-digit code I sent to your phone"
Never share verification codes. That code can let someone take over a WhatsApp account.

blocks.title: Never ask for, or share, PINs, OTPs or passwords
blocks.text: A real business never needs a customer's card PIN, one-time password (OTP), banking password or WhatsApp verification code. Put this in your payment quick reply. Also turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp settings for the business number.

blocks.title: Worked example: spotting a fake alert
blocks.context: For example, Bisi handles orders for a phone accessories shop in Abuja. A new customer orders 4 power banks at ₦18,000 each and sends a screenshot showing a ₦72,000 transfer. He asks for urgent dispatch because he is "travelling in one hour".
steps: Bisi checks the order total: 4 × ₦18,000 = ₦72,000. The amount matches.
She replies: "Thank you, Emeka. We will dispatch as soon as the payment reflects in our business account. I am confirming now."
She asks the owner to check the business bank app. After 20 minutes, no money has arrived.
She replies politely: "We have not received the transfer yet. Please check with your bank. We will dispatch once it reflects."
The customer becomes aggressive and then stops replying. Bisi labels the chat and notes it in the tracking sheet.
blocks.result: No goods were lost. The urgency, the screenshot and the pressure were warning signs; the business account was the only proof that counted.

blocks.title: Safe versus risky habits
items: Safe agent
Risky agent
blocks.caption: The left-hand habits protect customers and the business.

blocks.text: Professional boundaries
Customers may message at midnight, send many voice notes, or use insulting words. You are allowed to protect yourself while staying professional.

items: Use the away message for out-of-hours times and reply during working hours.

If a customer uses abusive language, stay calm and set a limit once: "I want to help you solve this. I can continue when we keep the conversation respectful." If it continues, escalate to your supervisor.
Never argue in public comments. Invite the customer to a private chat: "I am sorry about this. Please send us a message with your order number so we can sort it out."
Any threat of harm should go straight to your supervisor or the owner. Do not handle threats alone.

blocks.title: Keep a record
blocks.text: Whatever happens, write it in your tracking sheet with the date and time. Records protect you if a customer later disputes what was said.

takeaways: Collect only the personal data you need and keep it secure.
Payment is confirmed in the business account, never by screenshot.
Never ask for or share PINs, OTPs, passwords or verification codes.
Set limits on abuse calmly and escalate threats.

activity.title: Make your safety kit
steps: Turn on two-step verification on the support WhatsApp number.
Write a payment quick reply that names the official account type and says you never ask for PINs or codes.
Write a calm one-line boundary message for abusive chats.
List the personal details the business truly needs for an order, and cross out anything extra.
activity.evidence: A note or screenshot showing your payment reply, boundary message and the data-needed list.

quiz.q: A customer emails asking for a refund of ₦30,000 for a damaged blender. What is the best channel approach?
options: Reply only by voice note so it feels personal
Acknowledge quickly and keep the refund details confirmed in writing and logged
Ignore it until the owner reads emails
Move the conversation to a public comment
quiz.explain: Money matters need a clear written record and logging, while still getting a fast first reply.

quiz.q: Which WhatsApp Business feature lets you insert a saved answer by typing / and a shortcut?
quiz.explain: Quick replies are triggered with / followed by the shortcut word you chose.

quiz.q: A new customer sends a transfer screenshot and pushes for urgent dispatch. What should the agent do first?
options: Dispatch immediately to keep the customer happy
Ask for the customer's bank PIN to confirm
Confirm the money is in the business account before releasing goods
quiz.explain: Screenshots can be faked. Only the business account balance proves payment.

quiz.q: At 5 pm, Chika opens the label "Waiting for us" and sees 3 chats. What does this tell her?
options: 3 cases still need action from the business
quiz.explain: "Waiting for us" means the next step belongs to the business: these are open promises.

quiz.q: Which of these is the most appropriate greeting message?
options: "We reply instantly 24/7!" when the shop has one staff member
"Hello, thank you for your message. Please share your name and what you need; we reply within 30 minutes, Mon to Sat, 8 am to 6 pm."
quiz.explain: A good greeting is warm, sets an honest reply time and asks for useful details.

quiz.q: Why should an agent remove names and phone numbers before using a real chat in a portfolio?
options: Because customer personal data must not be shared without a proper reason
quiz.explain: Data protection principles mean you do not share a customer's personal data for your own purposes.

modules.title: Guided practice: workflow, writing and complaints
modules.overview: Learn the six-step workflow for every request, write replies and templates that customers understand the first time, and calm angry customers using the LAST method with realistic scripts.

lessons.title: The support workflow: acknowledge, clarify, resolve, confirm
objectives: Apply a six-step workflow to any support request
Ask clarifying questions that get the facts in one message
Decide when to solve a request yourself and when to escalate it
Close a case properly with a confirmation message

blocks.text: Good agents do not just "reply to messages". They move each request through the same steps every time, so nothing is missed and every customer gets the same quality. In Lesson 1.1 you saw the six stages. Now you will learn exactly what to do and say at each one.

blocks.name: manage-chats
blocks.alt: A person organising several chat conversations
blocks.caption: A repeatable workflow lets you handle many chats without losing track.

blocks.text: Step 1: Acknowledge quickly

The first reply tells the customer a human has seen them. It should come fast, even if you cannot solve the problem yet. Use their name, thank them and say what you are doing: "Hello Kemi, thank you for your message. I am checking your order now." A fast acknowledgement buys you time to do the real work properly.
Step 2: Clarify in one message
Many chats drag on because the agent asks one question at a time. Instead, ask for everything you need in a single, numbered message. Customers find numbered questions easy to answer on a phone.

blocks.title: Worked example: one clear clarifying message
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma supports an online shoe store in Port Harcourt. A customer writes: "The shoes you sent are wrong."
steps: Ifeoma acknowledges: "Hello Seyi, I am sorry about this. Let me fix it for you."
She sends one clarifying message: "To help quickly, please send: 1) your order number or the name used for the order, 2) a photo of the shoes you received, 3) the size and colour you ordered."
Seyi replies within 10 minutes with all three answers: order 2231, photo shows size 40, she ordered 41.
Ifeoma checks the order sheet: the order says 41. The warehouse packed the wrong size.
blocks.result: One message collected all the facts. Without it, Ifeoma would have needed three separate back-and-forth questions, and the customer would have waited longer.

blocks.text: Step 3: Check before you answer

Never guess. Check the order record, stock list, delivery notes or policy before replying. If you do not know, say "Let me confirm that for you" and find out. A wrong confident answer ("Your parcel arrives tomorrow") causes a second complaint when it does not.
Step 4: Solve or escalate

Decide whether you can solve the problem yourself. Each business should have simple rules about what agents can approve. For example, an agent might be allowed to arrange a free exchange for a wrong item, but need the owner's approval for any cash refund.

head: You can usually solve
You should escalate
rows: Price, stock and delivery questions
Refunds and money returned to customers
Order status updates from the record
Legal threats or threats of harm
Exchanges within the business's written policy
Requests outside policy (for example, a refund after the return period)
Resending invoices or instructions
Suspected fraud or a product safety issue

blocks.text: When you escalate, write a short summary so your supervisor does not need to read the whole chat: **who, what, what you have checked, what the customer wants, and the deadline**. Then tell the customer who is handling it and when they will hear back.
Step 5: Confirm with the customer

When the solution is in place, confirm it clearly and check it worked: "Your size 41 has been sent with our rider today. He will call you before delivery. Please return the size 40 to him. Is there anything else I can help with?" After delivery, a short check ("Did the new pair fit well?") shows care and tells you whether the case is truly solved.
Step 6: Log and close

Record the case in your tracking sheet with the date, channel, problem, action and outcome, and change the label to Resolved. You will build that sheet in Module 3. Logging only takes a minute but it is what lets you measure your work later.

blocks.title: The six-step support cycle
items: Acknowledge
Clarify
Check
Solve or escalate
Confirm
Log
blocks.caption: Logged cases feed back into better quick replies and fewer repeat problems.

blocks.title: Give a time, not just a promise
blocks.text: "I will get back to you soon" means nothing. "I will update you by 3 pm today" is specific. Set a phone reminder for every time you promise.
Handling several chats at once

On a busy day you may have five or more chats open together. Work in short rounds: acknowledge every new chat first, then go back and work on the one with the highest priority. Use labels so you can see which chats are waiting for you. Do not leave a customer mid-conversation for long without a word; if you need 20 minutes to check something, say so: "I am still checking with the warehouse and will reply by 11:30." Customers accept waiting much more easily when they know what is happening and when to expect you.

items: **Escalation summary template:** Customer: Seyi (order 2231). Issue: sent size 40, ordered 41. Checked: order sheet says 41, warehouse error. Customer wants: exchange. Deadline: promised update by 3 pm.
**Close message template:** "I am glad this is sorted, [name]. Thank you for your patience. If anything else comes up, just message us here."

takeaways: Acknowledge fast, then do the real work.
Ask all clarifying questions in one numbered message.
Check records before answering; never guess.
Escalate with a short summary and always log the case.

activity.title: Run one case through the six steps
steps: Take one real or realistic request (for example, a late delivery).
Write your acknowledgement and your single clarifying message.
Write what you would check and where.
Decide: solve or escalate. If escalating, write the five-part summary.
Write the confirmation and close messages.
activity.evidence: A written case sheet showing all six steps with your actual messages.

lessons.title: Writing replies that work: templates, tone and structure
objectives: Structure a chat reply and a support email so they are easy to read
Adjust tone from formal to friendly without losing professionalism
Turn negative news into a clear, positive next step
Build a reusable template library for common situations

blocks.text: Most support work is writing. Clear writing saves time because the customer understands the first time and does not need to ask again. Good support writing is **short, specific, warm and action-focused**.

blocks.name: compose-email
blocks.alt: A person writing an email on a laptop
blocks.caption: A clear structure makes every reply easier to write and easier to read.

blocks.text: The structure of a good reply

items: **Greet and use their name:** "Hello Amina,"
**Acknowledge the request or feeling:** "Thank you for letting us know your order is late. I understand you needed it for Saturday."
**Give the answer or action:** "I have checked with our dispatch team. Your parcel is in Abuja and will be delivered tomorrow, Thursday, before 4 pm."
**State the next step:** "The rider will call you on 0803 xxx xxxx before arriving."
**Close warmly:** "Thank you for your patience. I am here if you need anything else."

blocks.title: Reply structure, most important first
items: Answer or action
Next step and time
Acknowledgement
Greeting and close
blocks.caption: Put the answer near the top; customers on phones may not read to the end.

blocks.text: Chat versus email

On WhatsApp or chat, keep messages to 2 to 4 short lines and send one idea per message if the topic is complex. Avoid sending ten tiny messages in a row; it floods the customer's phone. In email, use a clear subject, short paragraphs, and bullet points for steps or details. Email can be a little more formal: "Dear Mr Okafor" for a first formal complaint, "Hello Chidi" once you are in a friendly thread.
Tone: warm, calm, professional

head: Instead of
Write
rows: "You did not read the delivery policy."
"Our delivery to your area takes 3 to 5 working days. I am sorry this was not clear when you ordered."
"That is not our problem."
"Let me see what I can do to help."
"We can't deliver on Sunday."
"We deliver Monday to Saturday. Would Monday morning work for you?"
"Calm down."
"I can see this has been frustrating, and I want to sort it out."
"ASAP"
"by 2 pm today"

blocks.text: Notice the patterns. Replace blame with explanation. Replace "can't" with what you **can** do. Replace vague time words with real times. Use "I" when you are taking action ("I have checked") and "we" for the business's rules ("We deliver Monday to Saturday").

blocks.title: Emojis and pidgin
blocks.text: A single friendly emoji can soften a chat with a happy customer, but avoid emojis in complaints, refunds or formal emails. Match the customer's language where the business allows: if a customer writes in pidgin and your brand voice is relaxed, a light, respectful reply in the same style can build rapport. If unsure, use simple standard English.
Templates for common situations
Write templates once, test them, and save them as quick replies or email drafts. Here are four you will use often.

items: **Delay:** "Hello [name], I am sorry your order is taking longer than expected. It is currently [status]. The new delivery date is [day, time]. I will message you as soon as it leaves our office."

**Out of stock:** "Thank you for your interest, [name]. The [item] is out of stock right now. We expect new stock on [date]. I can reserve one for you, or suggest [alternative] which is available today."
**Need more information:** "To help you quickly, please send: 1) [detail], 2) [detail], 3) [detail]."

**Cannot do what they ask:** "I understand why you are asking for [request]. We are not able to [request] because [short honest reason]. What I can do is [option 1] or [option 2]. Which would you prefer?"

blocks.title: Worked example: rewriting a weak reply
blocks.context: For example, a customer asks a catering business in Lagos: "Can you do jollof for 80 guests on 14th?" The first draft reply was: "Yes we can do it, price depends, send details."
steps: Problem 1: "price depends" gives no information. Fix: give a starting price per head and what changes it.
Problem 2: "send details" is vague. Fix: list the exact details needed.

Rewrite: "Hello Mrs Bello, thank you for thinking of us! Yes, we are available on the 14th. For 80 guests, jollof rice with chicken starts from about ₦3,500 per head, so roughly ₦280,000 (80 × ₦3,500), before delivery and serving staff."
Second message: "To give you an exact quote, please send: 1) venue area, 2) serving time, 3) whether you need servers and packs. I will send the quote within 2 hours of receiving these."
blocks.result: The rewritten reply answers the question, shows the calculation, lists exactly what is needed and gives a time for the quote. The customer can decide immediately.

blocks.title: Check templates before sending
blocks.text: The most common template mistake is sending one with a placeholder still in it, such as "Hello [name]" or the wrong price. Read every reply once before pressing send.

takeaways: Structure: greet, acknowledge, answer, next step, close.
Keep chat replies to a few short lines; use bullets in email.
Replace blame with explanation and vague words with real times.
Save tested templates and personalise every use.

activity.title: Build your template library
steps: Write the four templates above for the business you support, filling in real policies.
Rewrite three weak replies from past chats using the five-part structure.
Read each aloud: does it sound like a kind, capable person?
Save the templates as quick replies or email drafts.

lessons.title: Handling complaints and de-escalating angry customers
objectives: Use the LAST method (Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank) in written support
Write an apology that is sincere without admitting fault you cannot confirm
Offer choices to move an angry customer towards a solution
Respond to a public negative review professionally

blocks.text: Every business gets complaints. A complaint handled well can turn an angry customer into a loyal one, because they see how the business behaves when things go wrong. A complaint handled badly can spread to the customer's friends and to public reviews. This lesson gives you a simple method and real scripts.

blocks.name: angry-face
blocks.caption: Behind most angry messages is a real problem and a person who feels ignored.

blocks.text: Why customers get angry

Customers usually become angry when three things combine: something went wrong, they feel it was not their fault, and they think nobody is listening. You cannot always undo the first two, but you can fix the third immediately. That alone lowers the temperature.
The LAST method
A widely taught customer service approach is **LAST: Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank**. It was designed for face-to-face and phone service, but it works well in writing.

head: Step
What it means in writing
Example line
rows: Listen
Read the whole message, including voice notes, before replying. Repeat the key facts back.
"So the cake arrived with the top damaged, two hours before your daughter's party. I understand how upsetting that is."
Apologise
Say sorry for the experience, sincerely and once. No excuses in the first line.
"I am truly sorry this happened on such an important day."
Solve
Offer a concrete fix or choices, with times.
"I can send a replacement cake by 4 pm, or refund the cake in full. Which would you prefer?"
Thank
Thank them for telling you and for their patience.
"Thank you for letting us know straight away. It helps us fix it."

blocks.title: LAST in a written complaint
items: Listen and restate facts
Apologise once, sincerely
Offer a fix or choices
Thank and follow up
blocks.caption: Restating facts shows you listened; choices give the customer back some control.

blocks.text: Apologising without guessing fault

You can apologise for the customer's experience before you know whose fault it was. "I am sorry your parcel has not arrived" is honest. Avoid "It was our rider's fault" until you have checked; you might be wrong, and blaming a colleague or partner looks unprofessional. Once facts are confirmed, own the business's mistakes plainly: "We packed the wrong size. That was our error."
Language that calms and language that inflames

items: Calming: "I understand", "Let me fix this", "Here is what I can do", "You are right to expect better", "I will update you by 3 pm".
Inflaming: "Calm down", "As I said before", "That's our policy" (with no explanation), "You should have", silence for hours.
Avoid capital letters and many exclamation marks; in text they read as shouting.

blocks.title: Worked example: a full de-escalation chat
blocks.context: For example, Mariam supports a hair products shop in Ibadan. A customer, Tola, sends at 10:05 am: "THIS IS THE THIRD TIME I AM MESSAGING. I PAID ₦12,500 LAST WEEK AND NOTHING. YOU PEOPLE ARE SCAMMERS."
steps: 10:07 Listen and restate: "Hello Tola, I can see you paid ₦12,500 last week and have not received your order, and that you have had to message three times. I am sorry, that is not the service you should get."
10:08 Clarify: "Please send the name or phone number used for the order so I can find it immediately."
10:20 After checking: the order was packed but the address was missing a street name, so the rider could not deliver. Mariam does not blame the customer.

10:22 Solve with choices: "Your order is packed and ready. The rider could not find the address. Can you confirm your full address and a landmark? I can have it delivered today by 5 pm, or you can pick it up at our shop from 11 am."
10:25 Tola sends the address. 10:26 Thank: "Thank you, Tola. Delivery is booked for today before 5 pm. I will message you when the rider leaves."
2:40 pm: Mariam sends the rider's departure update. Next day: "Did everything arrive well?" Tola replies with a thank-you.
blocks.result: The customer went from accusing the business of fraud to thanking it within one day. Mariam also adds a step to her workflow: confirm full address and landmark at order time.

blocks.text: Public complaints and reviews

If a customer complains in a public comment or review, reply publicly once, briefly and politely, then move details to a private chat. Never argue in public or share order details there. Example: "Hello Tola, we are sorry about the delay with your order. We have sent you a message so we can fix this today." Other readers judge the business by this reply more than by the complaint.

blocks.title: When to stop and escalate
blocks.text: If a customer threatens harm, legal action, or a public campaign, or if the problem involves a product safety issue such as a skin reaction or food illness, escalate to your supervisor or the owner immediately and log it.

takeaways: LAST: Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank.
Restate the facts to prove you listened.
Apologise for the experience; confirm fault before naming it.
Offer choices with times, then follow up.
Reply to public complaints briefly and move details to private.

activity.title: Practise a de-escalation
steps: Write a realistic angry message a customer might send to the business you support.
Write your reply using all four LAST steps.
Underline any word that might inflame and rewrite it.
Write a short public reply to a negative review of the same problem.
Ask a friend to read both as the customer and tell you how they feel.
activity.evidence: The angry message, your LAST reply, the public reply and your friend's feedback.

quiz.q: A customer writes "My order is wrong." What is the most efficient next message after acknowledging?
options: One numbered message asking for order number, a photo and what was ordered
"That is impossible, we check every order"
quiz.explain: Asking for all needed facts in one numbered message saves time for both sides.

quiz.q: Which escalation summary is best?
options: "Seyi, order 2231: received size 40, ordered 41. Sheet confirms 41. Wants exchange. Update promised by 3 pm."
quiz.explain: A good summary covers who, what, what was checked, what the customer wants and the deadline.

quiz.q: Which line follows the advice on tone?
options: "We deliver Monday to Saturday. Would Monday morning work for you?"
quiz.explain: It replaces "can't" with what the business can do and offers a choice.

quiz.q: A caterer quotes ₦3,500 per head for 120 guests. What should the reply show as the rough total before delivery?
quiz.explain: 120 × ₦3,500 = ₦420,000. Showing the calculation makes the quote clear.

quiz.q: In the LAST method, what comes after Apologise?
quiz.explain: The order is Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank.

quiz.q: A customer posts a public complaint about a late order. What is the best response?
options: Explain publicly that the customer gave a wrong address
Reply briefly and politely in public, then continue in a private message
quiz.explain: Keep the public reply short and polite, and move details, including personal information, to private chat.

quiz.q: Before you have checked, which apology is most appropriate?
options: "I am sorry your parcel has not arrived. Let me check right now."
"Sorry, but it is not our fault."
quiz.explain: Apologise for the experience without guessing whose fault it is.

modules.title: Quality and evidence: tracking, policies and metrics
modules.overview: Track every request as a ticket in a sheet or free help desk, keep answers honest and consistent with policies, FAQs and escalation rules, and measure your work with first response time, resolution rate, FCR and CSAT.

lessons.title: Ticket tracking with a simple sheet or a free help-desk tool
objectives: Explain what a support ticket is and why every case needs one
Build a ticket tracking sheet with the right columns
Use statuses and priorities to decide what to work on next
Decide when a free help-desk tool is worth moving to

blocks.text: A **ticket** is simply a record of one customer request, from the moment it arrives until it is closed. Big companies use help-desk software. A small business can do the same job with a free spreadsheet such as Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel. What matters is that every case is written down in the same way, so nobody forgets a customer and you can measure your work.

blocks.name: spreadsheet
blocks.alt: A person working with a spreadsheet
blocks.caption: A simple sheet turns scattered chats into a list you can manage and measure.

blocks.text: The columns your sheet needs

head: Column
Example entry
Why it matters
rows: Ticket ID
A unique number to refer to the case
Date and time received
Needed to calculate first response time
Customer (first name, contact)
Kemi, WhatsApp
To find the chat again
Channel
WhatsApp / Email / Instagram
Shows where requests come from
Category
Delivery, Wrong item, Payment, Product question
Shows the most common problems
Priority
High / Normal / Low
Decides what to handle first
First reply time
For first response time
Status
New / Waiting for customer / Waiting for us / Resolved
Shows what still needs action
Resolved time
For resolution time
Notes and outcome
Exchange sent, customer confirmed
Your evidence of what happened

blocks.text: In Google Sheets, use **Data validation** (a dropdown list) for Channel, Category, Priority and Status so everyone types the same words. Then you can use a **filter** to show only "Waiting for us" tickets, or only High priority ones. Freeze the top row so the headings stay visible as you scroll.
Setting priorities

items: **High:** money taken but no goods, safety issues (for example a skin reaction to a product), a customer who has already chased twice, anything with a same-day deadline.
**Normal:** wrong item, late delivery inside a reasonable time, most complaints.
**Low:** general questions, feedback, requests for future products.

blocks.title: Deciding what to handle first
items: Urgent and serious: do now
Serious, not urgent: schedule today
Urgent, minor: quick reply
Neither: batch later
blocks.caption: Sort each ticket by how serious it is and how urgent it is.

blocks.title: Worked example: a day's ticket sheet
blocks.context: For example, Ruth supports a baby products shop in Abuja. On Tuesday she logs 8 tickets in her Google Sheet.
steps: T-0201 to T-0204: four product questions, priority Low, answered and resolved within an hour.
T-0205: customer paid ₦23,000 two days ago, no delivery yet. Priority High. Ruth chases dispatch, delivery booked for the afternoon.
T-0206: wrong colour of baby carrier. Priority Normal. Exchange arranged for Thursday; status Waiting for us.

T-0207: customer reports a rash after using a baby lotion. Priority High. Ruth asks for the batch number, advises the customer to stop using it and seek medical advice, and escalates to the owner immediately.
T-0208: request for a twin stroller the shop does not stock. Priority Low, resolved with an honest answer and a suggestion.
At 5:30 pm she filters Status = Waiting for us and sees T-0206 and T-0207 still open. She adds next actions and reminder times.
blocks.result: Ruth closed 6 of 8 tickets the same day, and the two open ones have clear next steps. Nothing depends on her memory.

blocks.text: Moving to a free help-desk tool

When several people answer customers, or volume grows beyond what a sheet comfortably handles, a help-desk tool helps. Tools such as **Freshdesk** and **Zoho Desk** offer free plans for small teams (check each provider's website for current limits, because plans change). A help desk turns emails into tickets automatically, assigns them to agents, tracks statuses and calculates metrics for you.

head: Simple sheet
Free help-desk tool
rows: Free, works offline in Excel, easy to start
Free plan for small teams, but needs internet and setup time
You enter every ticket by hand
Email requests become tickets automatically
Metrics need simple formulas
Reports on response and resolution time are built in
Best for 1 to 2 people and modest volume
Better for teams and higher volume

blocks.text: A daily routine for your sheet

items: Morning: log any messages that arrived overnight, with their real received times.
During the day: add each new ticket as you acknowledge it, not at the end of the day when details are forgotten.
Each time a case moves, update the Status and add a short note, such as "exchange booked for Thu".
Evening: filter for open tickets, check every promised update time, and set reminders for tomorrow.

blocks.text: Protect the sheet like any other customer data. Share it only with colleagues who need it, use the sharing settings to control who can edit, and avoid storing full bank details or ID numbers in it. A first name, contact channel and order number are usually enough to find a case again.

blocks.title: Start with the sheet
blocks.text: Even if you plan to use a help desk later, a sheet teaches you what to track. Employers are often impressed when a candidate can show a clean, well-designed tracking sheet with real metrics.

takeaways: A ticket is one request tracked from arrival to closure.
Record received time, first reply time and resolved time for metrics.
Use dropdowns for channel, category, priority and status.
Review "Waiting for us" tickets every day.
Move to a free help-desk tool when the team or volume grows.

activity.title: Build your ticket tracker
steps: Create a Google Sheet or Excel file with the ten columns above.
Add dropdown lists for Channel, Category, Priority and Status.
Log at least 10 real or realistic tickets with times.
Filter to show only open tickets and write the next action for each.
activity.evidence: Your tracking sheet with 10 logged tickets (screenshot or file).

lessons.title: Policies, FAQs and escalation: keeping support honest and consistent
objectives: Write a clear FAQ and a short support policy for refunds, exchanges and delivery
Apply escalation rules consistently
Avoid dishonest support practices such as false promises and hiding problems
Handle product safety complaints responsibly

blocks.text: Customers trust a business that gives the same answer every time and keeps its word. That consistency comes from three written things: a **support policy**, a set of **FAQs**, and **escalation rules**. Without them, each agent makes up answers, and customers notice.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking off a checklist
blocks.caption: Written policies mean every customer gets the same fair answer.

blocks.text: A one-page support policy
Ask the business owner to agree these points in writing. If you are the owner, decide them now. Keep the language simple enough to paste into a chat.

items: **Delivery:** areas covered, usual delivery times, who pays delivery, what happens if the customer is not available.
**Exchanges:** within how many days, condition of item (unused, with tags), who pays return delivery.
**Refunds:** when a refund is given, how (to the original payment account), who approves it, and how long processing takes.
**Damaged or wrong items:** what proof is needed (photo within a set time) and the remedy offered.
**Response times:** working hours and the first reply time customers can expect.

blocks.title: Consumer rights exist
blocks.text: Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018 protects consumers and is enforced by the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC). A business policy cannot simply remove a customer's basic rights. If you are unsure whether a policy is fair, the owner should seek proper advice.
FAQs: answer once, use many times

An FAQ (frequently asked questions) list collects the answers to the questions you get every day. Use your ticket sheet's Category column to find them: the categories with the most tickets are your FAQ topics. Put the FAQ on the website, in a WhatsApp catalogue description, or as a pinned post, and turn each answer into a quick reply.

blocks.title: Worked example: building FAQs from ticket data
blocks.context: For example, Funmi reviews her tracking sheet for one month: 120 tickets in total.
steps: She counts tickets by category: Delivery time 42, Payment methods 25, Sizes 18, Wrong item 15, Product questions 12, Other 8.
Delivery time is 42 ÷ 120 = 0.35, so 35% of all tickets. Payment is 25 ÷ 120 ≈ 21%. Sizes are 18 ÷ 120 = 15%.
Those three categories together are 85 tickets, about 71% of the month's work.
She writes three FAQ answers (delivery areas and times, accepted payment methods, size guide with measurements) and adds them to the website and quick replies.
She also tells the owner that 15 wrong-item tickets suggest a packing check is needed.
blocks.result: Funmi now has evidence for where to focus. Clear FAQs should reduce repeated questions, and the next month's sheet will show whether they did.

blocks.text: A good FAQ answer is short, specific and complete. For example: "**How long does delivery take?** Within Lagos, 1 to 2 working days after payment is confirmed. Other states, 3 to 5 working days through our courier. Delivery fees depend on your area, and we confirm the fee before you pay." Review your FAQs every month against new ticket data. If a question keeps coming in even though it is in the FAQ, the answer may be unclear or hard to find, so rewrite it or move it somewhere more visible, such as the greeting message.
Escalation rules

blocks.title: Escalation levels for a complaint
items: Agent resolves within policy
Supervisor approves exceptions
Owner handles refunds, legal, safety
blocks.caption: Each level has clear limits, so customers get fast answers and big decisions get the right approval.

blocks.text: Write down who handles what and how fast. For example: agent can approve exchanges within policy; supervisor approves anything outside policy within 1 working day; owner handles all refunds above an agreed amount, legal threats and safety issues the same day. The point is not bureaucracy: it is so the customer gets a quick, correct answer.
Honesty in support

items: **Do not promise what you cannot control.** Say "The courier estimates Thursday" rather than "It will definitely arrive Thursday".
**Do not hide known problems.** If a batch is delayed, tell waiting customers before they chase you.
**Do not fake reviews or pressure customers to delete complaints.** Fix the problem instead.
**Do not make up reasons.** "I will find out and update you by 2 pm" is always better than an invented answer.

blocks.text: Product safety complaints

If a customer reports harm (a skin reaction to a cosmetic, illness after food, an electric shock from a device), treat it as High priority. Express concern, advise them to stop using the product and to seek medical help if needed, ask for the product name, batch number and photos, and escalate to the owner immediately. Do not argue or say "Nobody else has complained". Regulated products such as food, drugs and cosmetics fall under NAFDAC in Nigeria, and the owner may need to act on the batch.

blocks.title: Do not give medical advice
blocks.text: As a support agent, you are not a health professional. Advise the customer to stop using the product and see a doctor or pharmacist if they have symptoms. Do not suggest treatments.

takeaways: Agree a one-page written policy for delivery, exchanges, refunds and response times.
Build FAQs from your most common ticket categories.
Escalation rules say who decides what, and how fast.
Never promise what you cannot control or invent answers.
Treat safety complaints as high priority and escalate at once.

activity.title: Write your policy, FAQs and escalation rules
steps: Draft a one-page support policy covering the five points in this lesson.
Count your tickets by category and pick the top three FAQ topics.
Write a clear FAQ answer for each.
Write three escalation levels with names and time limits.
activity.evidence: Your policy page, three FAQ answers and escalation rules.

lessons.title: Support metrics: first response time, resolution rate and satisfaction
objectives: Define and calculate first response time and average resolution time
Calculate resolution rate, first contact resolution and CSAT
Use spreadsheet formulas to calculate metrics from your ticket sheet
Write a short weekly support report with findings and actions

blocks.text: Metrics turn "I work hard" into evidence: "This week I handled 64 tickets, with an average first response time of 18 minutes and a resolution rate of 92%." Help-desk tools calculate these automatically, but you should understand exactly how, so you can calculate them from a simple sheet and explain them to an employer.

blocks.name: bar-chart
blocks.caption: Numbers from your ticket sheet show what is working and what needs fixing.

blocks.text: The five core metrics

head: Metric
What it measures
Formula
rows: First response time (FRT)
How long customers wait for the first human reply
First reply time minus time received; average = total of all FRTs ÷ number of tickets
Average resolution time
How long it takes to fully solve a case
Resolved time minus time received; average over resolved tickets
Resolution rate
Share of tickets solved in the period
Resolved tickets ÷ tickets received × 100
First contact resolution (FCR)
Share solved in the first reply, with no back-and-forth
Tickets solved in one reply ÷ resolved tickets × 100
Customer satisfaction (CSAT)
How happy customers were
Satisfied responses (for example 4 or 5 out of 5) ÷ all survey responses × 100

blocks.text: Automatic greeting and away messages do **not** count as a first response. FRT measures when a person actually replied. Many businesses measure FRT only within working hours, so a message at 11 pm counts from 8 am the next day; decide your rule and state it in your report.

blocks.title: Worked example: first response time
blocks.context: For example, Ada logs 5 WhatsApp tickets on Monday morning (working hours start 8:00 am).
steps: Ticket 1: received 8:05, first reply 8:12 = 7 minutes.
Ticket 2: received 8:20, first reply 8:45 = 25 minutes.
Ticket 3: received 9:10, first reply 9:16 = 6 minutes.
Ticket 4: received 10:02, first reply 10:50 = 48 minutes.
Ticket 5: received 10:30, first reply 10:44 = 14 minutes.
Total = 7 + 25 + 6 + 48 + 14 = 100 minutes. Average FRT = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 minutes.
blocks.result: Average FRT is 20 minutes. Ticket 4 (48 minutes) pulled the average up; Ada notes she was in a meeting then, and plans to check chats between meetings.

blocks.title: Worked example: resolution rate, FCR and CSAT for a week
blocks.context: For example, Ada's weekly totals: 80 tickets received, 72 resolved by Friday, 45 of those solved in the first reply. She sent a 1 to 5 rating question to resolved customers and got 40 responses: 22 gave 5, 12 gave 4, 4 gave 3, 2 gave 1.
steps: Resolution rate = 72 ÷ 80 × 100 = 90%.
Response rate to the survey = 40 ÷ 72 × 100 ≈ 56%, which she reports so readers know how many customers answered.
blocks.result: Ada's week: 90% resolution rate, 62.5% first contact resolution, 85% CSAT. The 8 unresolved tickets carry over to next week and must be listed.

blocks.text: Formulas in Google Sheets or Excel

If column B holds received time and column G holds first reply time (as full date and time), put **=(G2-B2)*24*60** in a new column to get minutes, because spreadsheets store time as fractions of a day. Then use **=AVERAGE(K2:K81)** for the average FRT. Count resolved tickets with **=COUNTIF(H2:H81,"Resolved")** and divide by **=COUNTA(A2:A81)** for the resolution rate.

blocks.title: From ticket sheet to report
items: Log times and status
Calculate with formulas
Compare with last week
Find the cause
Agree one action
blocks.caption: Metrics are only useful when they lead to an action.

blocks.text: Reading metrics honestly

items: An average can hide problems. Also look at the longest wait and how many tickets waited over your target (for example, over 30 minutes).
Do not chase one number at the cost of another. Closing tickets too quickly to raise the resolution rate, without truly solving them, will lower CSAT and bring repeat complaints.
Small numbers swing a lot. A CSAT of 100% from 3 responses tells you little; always report how many responses you had.
Compare like with like: this week against last week, same channel, same rules.

blocks.text: A short weekly report

Keep it to half a page: the numbers, one sentence on what changed, the top ticket categories, and one or two actions. For example: "Week 40: 80 tickets (up from 66). Average FRT 20 min (target 30). Resolution rate 90%. CSAT 85% from 40 responses. Top categories: delivery time 30%, wrong item 15%. Action: add delivery FAQ to greeting message; ask packing team to double-check sizes."

blocks.title: Ask for ratings simply
blocks.text: After closing a case, send: "Thank you, [name]. On a scale of 1 to 5, how happy are you with how we handled this? (5 = very happy)". Log the number in your sheet. Do not pressure customers to give a high score.

takeaways: FRT = first human reply time minus time received; automatic replies do not count.
Resolution rate = resolved ÷ received × 100.
FCR = solved in first reply ÷ resolved × 100.
CSAT = satisfied responses ÷ all responses × 100; report the number of responses.
Every report should end with an action.

activity.title: Calculate your metrics
steps: Use the tickets in your tracking sheet from Lesson 3.1 (at least 10).
Add a column that calculates first response time in minutes.
Calculate average FRT, resolution rate and FCR.
If you collected ratings, calculate CSAT and state the number of responses.
Write a half-page weekly report with one action.
activity.evidence: Your sheet with metric formulas and a half-page report.

quiz.q: Four tickets had first response times of 10, 30, 5 and 15 minutes. What is the average FRT?
In one week a team received 50 tickets and resolved 44. What is the resolution rate?
Of 60 resolved tickets, 39 were solved in the first reply. What is the first contact resolution rate?
A customer messages at 10:00 pm. The away message is sent at once, and a human replies at 8:15 am. Under a working-hours rule starting at 8:00 am, what is the FRT?
options: 0 minutes, because of the away message
quiz.explain: Automatic messages do not count, and with a working-hours rule the clock starts at 8:00 am, so FRT is 15 minutes.

quiz.q: A customer reports a rash after using a body cream. What priority and action are correct?
options: High; advise stopping use and seeking medical help, collect batch details, escalate to the owner
High; tell her it is probably an allergy and suggest a treatment
quiz.explain: Safety complaints are High priority. Agents should not give medical advice but must escalate quickly.

quiz.q: Ticket categories for a month: Delivery 30, Payment 10, Sizes 20, Other 40 (100 total). Which topic should be the first FAQ?
quiz.explain: Delivery is the largest specific category (30%). "Other" is a mix of topics and should be broken down first.

quiz.q: CSAT this week is 100%, from 3 survey responses out of 70 resolved tickets. How should this be reported?
options: As 100% from only 3 responses, so not reliable; aim to collect more ratings
quiz.explain: Always report the number of responses. Three responses is too few to draw conclusions.

modules.title: Portfolio and impact: proof, jobs and your 90-day plan
modules.overview: Turn your work into a portfolio of documented interactions, prepare for remote support roles while avoiding job scams, and write a 90-day improvement plan based on your own metrics.

lessons.title: Building your support portfolio: three documented interactions
objectives: Select three interactions that show a range of support skills
Document each interaction with context, your replies and your reasoning
Anonymise customer data properly
Present your tracking sheet and metrics as evidence

blocks.text: A portfolio is proof. Anyone can write "good communication skills" on a CV. A short document showing three real or realistic conversations, your exact replies, and the reasons behind them, shows an employer or client how you actually work. This lesson shows you how to build it from what you have already created in this course.

blocks.name: portfolio
blocks.caption: Your portfolio shows how you think, not just what you say.

blocks.text: Choose three interactions
Pick interactions that show different skills. A strong set looks like this:

items: **A routine request handled efficiently:** for example a pre-sale question answered with a personalised quick reply and a link to the catalogue.
**A problem solved through the workflow:** for example a wrong item, showing your clarifying message, the check, the fix and the confirmation.
**A challenging interaction:** an angry customer, a refund outside policy, or a suspected scam, showing de-escalation or safe handling.

blocks.text: If you are not yet working in support, create realistic scenarios for a real type of business (a bakery, a fashion store, a phone shop) and role-play them with a friend who plays the customer. Label them clearly as practice scenarios. Honesty matters: never present a practice case as a real job.
How to document each interaction

head: Section
What to include
rows: Context
Business type, channel, customer's first message (anonymised), time received
Your replies
Your exact messages, in order, with times
Reasoning
Why you chose each step: what you checked, why you offered those choices, why you escalated or not
Outcome
How it ended, customer's response or rating, time to resolve
Reflection
One thing you would do differently and one change you suggested to the business

blocks.title: One portfolio case, start to finish
items: Context
Your replies with times
Reasoning
Outcome and rating
Reflection
blocks.caption: Each of your three cases follows this same five-part layout.

blocks.text: Anonymise properly

items: Replace customer names with a role or a different first name, and say so: "Customer A".
Remove phone numbers, addresses, account numbers and order numbers that could identify someone.
Crop or blur screenshots. Check the profile photo and the top bar of the chat.
If the business is a real employer, ask permission before sharing any of its internal documents.

blocks.title: Worked example: documenting a challenging case
blocks.context: For example, Grace practised with a friend playing a customer of a gadget shop who received a phone charger that does not work, and who was angry because it was a gift.
steps: Context: "Practice scenario. WhatsApp, 11:02 am. Customer A: 'The charger you sold me is useless. I bought it as a gift and now I am embarrassed.'"
Replies: 11:04 acknowledgement and apology; 11:05 one numbered clarifying message (order name, photo of charger connected, phone model); 11:20 offer of a replacement by 4 pm or refund.

Reasoning: "I restated the gift detail to show I listened. I offered two choices because the customer felt embarrassed and needed some control back. Refund needed owner approval, so I checked policy first."
Outcome: customer chose replacement; delivered 3:40 pm; rating 5 out of 5; resolution time 4 hours 38 minutes.
Reflection: "I would ask for the phone model at the time of sale next time. I suggested adding a 'test before dispatch' step."
blocks.result: The case shows the LAST method, the six-step workflow, policy awareness, a metric and a business improvement, all on one page.

blocks.text: Add your evidence pack

Attach your supporting tools after the three cases: a screenshot of your quick replies list, your ticket tracking sheet (with any personal data removed), your metric calculations and your weekly report. Together these show you can run a support process, not just write messages.
Write a short introduction

Open the portfolio with three or four sentences about you: the channels you have used, the kind of businesses you have supported, and the tools you can use. For example: "I support customers for small online shops on WhatsApp Business and email. I use quick replies, a Google Sheets ticket tracker and simple metrics to keep response times low. This portfolio shows three cases, my tracking sheet and a weekly report." Keep it factual; let the cases show your quality.

lessons.title: Remote support jobs: skills, tools and how to apply safely
objectives: Describe common remote customer support roles and what they involve
Identify the practical skills and set-up employers expect
Present your support experience in a CV and an interview
Recognise fake job offers and recruitment scams

blocks.text: Customer support is one of the jobs that can often be done remotely, from home, for businesses in Nigeria or abroad. Titles vary: **customer support representative, customer service agent, chat support agent, virtual assistant (with support duties), community manager**. Whatever the title, employers look for the skills you have practised in this course.

blocks.name: working-remotely
blocks.alt: A woman working remotely on a laptop
blocks.caption: Remote support work needs reliable tools, clear writing and good time habits.

blocks.text: What employers usually look for

head: Skill
How to show it
rows: Clear written English
Your portfolio cases and a well-written application
Calm handling of complaints
Your challenging case using LAST
Organisation
Your ticket tracking sheet with statuses and priorities
Comfort with tools
Google Sheets, email, WhatsApp Business; any help desk you have tried, such as a Freshdesk free plan
Understanding of metrics
Your FRT, resolution rate and CSAT calculations and report
Reliability
Stable internet plan, backup power, a quiet place to work

blocks.text: Your remote set-up

items: A working laptop is usually expected for full-time remote roles; some part-time WhatsApp support roles can be done on a smartphone.
Reliable internet with a backup (for example two different network SIMs or a mobile hotspot).
Backup power: a power bank for your phone and, if possible, a way to keep your laptop running during outages.
A headset if the role includes calls.
A quiet space and clear working hours agreed with your household.

blocks.text: Typing speed helps in chat roles. Free online typing tests let you check your speed in words per minute; practise regularly and note your improvement.
Presenting yourself

On your CV, write achievements with numbers rather than duties. Compare "Responsible for answering customers" with "Handled about 60 WhatsApp and email tickets per week for a skincare shop; average first response time 20 minutes; 90% resolution rate." Only use numbers you can back up from your sheet.

blocks.title: Worked example: answering a common interview question
blocks.context: For example, in a video interview for a chat support role, Zainab is asked: "Tell me about a time you dealt with an angry customer." She uses the STAR structure: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
steps: Situation: "A customer of the hair shop I support messaged in capitals saying we were scammers after paying ₦12,500 and waiting a week."
Task: "I needed to calm her, find the order and get it delivered."
Action: "I restated her problem and apologised, asked for her order name in one message, found the parcel was held because the address had no street name, and offered delivery that day or pick-up."
Result: "It was delivered that afternoon, she thanked us, and I added a landmark question to our order form so it would not happen again."
blocks.result: A clear, specific answer of about one minute that shows method, empathy and improvement. Zainab can point to the same case in her portfolio.

blocks.title: Real job versus likely scam
items: Genuine offer
Warning signs
blocks.caption: If an offer shows signs from the right column, stop and check before going further.
left: No fee to apply or start
right: Asks you to pay a fee
Asks for bank PIN or OTP

blocks.text: Avoiding recruitment scams

Job scams target people looking for remote work. Common tricks include asking for a "registration", "training" or "equipment" fee, offering very high pay for simple tasks, recruiting only through private chat with no company details, and asking for bank login details "to pay your salary". A genuine employer pays you; you do not pay them to work.

blocks.title: Check before you share
blocks.text: Search the company name with words like "scam" or "review". Check that the email comes from the company's own domain, not a free email account. Never share your BVN, card PIN, OTP or passwords during recruitment. If something feels rushed or secretive, pause and ask someone you trust.
A short application message

Many support roles are applied for by email or through a job site message. Your application is itself a writing test, so apply what you learned in Module 2: short paragraphs, specific facts, a clear next step. For example: "Dear Hiring Team, I am applying for the Chat Support Agent role. For the past six months I have handled WhatsApp and email support for a skincare shop, about 60 tickets a week, with an average first response time of 20 minutes. I track every case in a Google Sheet and write a weekly report. My portfolio is here: [link]. I am available for an interview any weekday. Thank you for your time. Ngozi." Replace the details with your own true numbers, and check the company name and role title before sending.
Where to look

Look on established job sites and professional networks such as LinkedIn, on the careers pages of companies you know, and through people in your network who already work in support. Local businesses that sell online often need part-time WhatsApp support and may be a good first step to build real, referenceable experience.

takeaways: Remote support roles use the same core skills under different titles.
Show skills with evidence: portfolio, tracking sheet, metrics.
Write CV achievements with numbers you can back up.
Use STAR to answer interview questions.
Never pay to get a job or share PINs, OTPs or passwords.
